implementation_notes: JavaScript's idiom is the options object with destructured per-property defaults: `function createServer({ host = 'localhost', port = 8080 } = {})` lets callers name only what they override, order stops mattering and adding a key never breaks existing calls. The `= {}` default on the whole parameter is load-bearing - without it a no-argument call throws on destructuring `undefined` - and the defaults must sit in the destructuring, not on the object literal, or any partial object silently drops the rest. When the option set must be stored, diffed or serialized, use the spread-merge over a defaults object instead.
pitfalls: Forgetting the outer `= {}` (or passing `undefined`) throws `TypeError: Cannot destructure property ... of 'undefined'` for the no-argument call.

Defaults written on the whole-object default (`function f(opts = { a: 1, b: 2 })`) are replaced wholesale by any partial object, so callers silently lose the other defaults; put defaults per property inside the destructuring.
A destructuring default fires only for `undefined`, not for `null`; the API must decide whether nullish means 'use the default' (`??`) or an error.
Unknown keys are ignored: a misspelled option is silently dropped unless something (TypeScript types, a schema check, an explicit key whitelist) catches it.

variants.name: Defaults object merged with object spread (ES2018)
variants.implementation_notes: Keep the defaults as an ordinary object and merge the caller's overrides with object spread: `const cfg = { ...defaults, ...overrides }`. The option set stays a data value that can be stored, logged, diffed and sent over the wire, and a missing key never throws - at the cost of a shallow merge that keeps explicit `undefined` values (so a caller spreading a partial object with `undefined` can blank a default) and no per-property type checking unless a validator runs afterwards. Use it when options are data rather than an API argument list.
pitfalls: Object spread is shallow: nested option objects are shared with the caller's object and can be mutated later through either reference.
An explicit `undefined` in the override object wins over the default, so callers who pass `{ tls: undefined }` unintentionally blank the setting.
No key checking happens at runtime, and without TypeScript a typo simply adds a key while the default stays in force.
